subject: Make the Basket
body:
![](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/f36e0cb3-0b64-4109-a0ce-28570e6f9fbc/makethebasket.png?t=1778846698)

Somewhere in Egypt, a mother sat with reeds in her hands.

Maybe it was early morning.

Maybe the house was quiet.

Maybe her baby boy was sleeping nearby while Pharaoh’s command hung over the land:

Every Hebrew baby boy was to be thrown into the Nile.

She could not change the law.

She could not storm the palace.

She could not fight Egypt.

She could not see the plagues, the Passover, the Red Sea, or the deliverance of a nation.

She could not see Moses.

Not yet.

All she could see was a baby.

And all she could make was a basket.

So she made it.

She wove the reeds.  
She covered it with pitch.  
She placed her son inside.  
She carried him to the water.

Then she released what she loved into a river she could not control.

That is faith.

Not feelings.

Not hype.

Not pretending you are not afraid.

Faith is trembling hands doing the next obedient thing.

The basket did not deliver Israel.

God did.

But the basket was her part.

And maybe that is where many of us get stuck.

We keep asking for the whole river.

God keeps asking for the basket. (Props to Pastor Petra for this insight on [Mother’s Day 2026 Message](https://youtu.be/N8BFmJeeQvY?si=QbjkIGSl3t50yYVz&utm_source=letters.batsirai.com&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=make-the-basket))

I have felt this recently with my daughter, Simmone.

She is planning to go to Christ For The Nations Institute in Dallas.

And honestly, it seems good.

It feels like one of those things with God’s fingerprints on it.

But then comes the question every parent knows:

### **How?**

How do we pay for it?

How do we plan it?

How do we get from here to there?

How do we protect her?

How do we know?

“How” sounds responsible.

And sometimes it is.

But sometimes “how” becomes fear dressed in a button-up shirt.

Sometimes “how” is where obedience goes to get delayed.

We want the whole map.

God gives the next instruction.

Mary understood this at the wedding in Cana.

The wine ran out.

The need was real.

The servants had no solution.

Mary did not explain the miracle.

She did not manage the outcome.

She simply said:

**“Do whatever He tells you.”**

That is the whole thing.

Make the basket.

Fill the jars.

Do whatever He says.

Not because the basket is impressive.

Not because the jars make sense.

Not because you know how the story ends.

But because obedience is enough for today.

Some of you are carrying a dream bigger than your current life.

A calling you cannot afford yet.

A song you have not finished.

A business you do not know how to launch.

A book you do not know how to write.

A child you cannot control.

A future you can see in your heart but cannot yet touch with your hands.

And the gap is loud.

Bank account says no.  
Calendar says no.  
Confidence says no.  
Experience says no.  
People say no.

But God may not be asking you to solve the whole calling today.

He may be asking:

### **What is the basket?**

For the worship leader, it may be the setlist you aren’t 100% sure about.

For the songwriter, the line that feels too vulnerable to share.

For the builder, the rough first version.

For the parent, the prayer over your child when you do not know how the story unfolds.

Small does not mean insignificant.

A basket can look ridiculous beside a river, or a Pharaoh

But obedience often looks small before it looks supernatural.

We want provision first.

Show me the money…

Tell me HOW, WHEN, WHAT, WHY, WHERE… HOW AGAIN?

Then obedience.

But sometimes provision meets us after the basket is in the water.

So make the basket.

Fill the jars.

Send the application.

Write the song.

Build the page.

Have the conversation.

Take the step.

Your basket is enough.

Not because it can carry the whole future.

Because God can.

And you are enough because you can make a basket.

**And your basket + God** can change the world, free captives, create a nation… save a child.

May you can’t fund, force, and figure out the whole calling.

Remember you belong to the One who can.

And trust Him - because He is good.

See you next Friday.

subject: Why I fear Instagram
body:
![](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/941135e0-cb6b-4d51-9716-3a2f30b35cb7/instgram-mirror.png?t=1779472370)

I don’t really like going on Instagram.

Not because Instagram is evil.

Because Instagram has faces.

People singing songs.  
Leading worship.  
Building things.  
Traveling.  
Creating.  
Doing the kind of things I thought I would be doing by now.

Twitter/X.com feels safer.

Instagram feels like a mirror.

Mirror, mirror on my screen, who’s the fairest that’s ever been…

Or maybe worse, a courtroom.

No one on the screen is accusing me.

They’re just living.

But somehow, by the time I’m done scrolling, I’m on trial.

Here is who you thought you would be.  
Here is what you said you wanted to do.  
Here is the song you never released.  
Here is the idea still sitting in your voice notes.  
Here is the thing you built but are still afraid to share.

And the hardest part is not even the comparison.

It’s what happens after.

I compare.

Then I feel bad for comparing.

Then I become my own accuser.

I should be better than this.  
I should be more mature.  
I should be more confident.  
I should have done more by now.  
I should not still be struggling with this.

So now I’m not just behind.

I’m ashamed that I feel behind.

That spiral is exhausting.

Especially when the thing I care about most is helping people know they are already loved.

That is the painful irony.

I am trying to teach children they are loved before they perform.

And yet some part of me still fears that if what I make is rejected, then maybe I am too.

I believe the message.

I’m still learning to receive it.

And maybe that’s the part I don’t want to admit.

Not publicly.

Not as someone who leads worship.

Not as someone who writes about beloved identity.

Not as someone who wants to encourage other people.

But maybe honesty is better than pretending I graduated from the lesson I’m still living inside of.

So maybe the question is not, “Why can’t I get over this?”

Maybe the question is:

What does Jesus think of me when I’m spiraling?

When I’m comparing.

When I’m hiding.

When I’m afraid.

When I’m turning someone else’s life into evidence against mine.

Does He join the accusation?

Does He look at me and say, “You should be further by now”?

I don’t think He does.

I think He sees the fear underneath the comparison.

The ache underneath the scrolling.

The part of me that still wonders if there is room for me.

And maybe He is not as disappointed in me as I am.

Maybe He is not standing over me with the voice of the accuser.

Maybe He is sitting with me in the middle of the spiral, gently telling the truth again:

You are not behind, My love.

I don’t have a clean ending for this.

I still avoid Instagram sometimes.

I still compare.

I still have voice notes full of things I haven’t released.

But maybe you do too.

And maybe today, that’s enough.

Not a solution.

Just a little less loneliness.

A little less accusation.

A little more room to breathe.  
  
See you next Friday

subject: The Parking Lot Test
previewText: There Must Be More Than This
body:
![](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/ea070e3b-8156-4e76-8a80-f3d9645b4b14/82BC9FD2-3A88-43F4-8148-5078FC120E0F.png?t=1780088214)

Last night, I went to a concert by a well-known worship artist.

And honestly, it was phenomenal.

The music was excellent.  
The room was full.  
The sound was huge.  
The moments were powerful.

There were times when the whole room was singing, hands lifted, voices strong, and you could feel that something meaningful was happening.

This is not a critique of the artist.

Not even close.

They served the room beautifully. The songs were strong. The musicianship was excellent. The heart behind it felt sincere.

If I had to nitpick… could have been more vertical/throne room moments. It was very horizontal/testimony/thanksgiving. Which is not wrong… just a little incomplete in my opinion.

But when it was over, I walked out to my car and noticed something in me that felt uncomfortable.

I didn’t feel marked.

I didn’t feel like I had just encountered Jesus in a way that changed how I saw Him, or myself, or the world.

I felt more like I had just watched a really good movie.

Moved? Yes.  
Inspired? Probably.  
Impressed? Definitely.

It wasn’t entertainment.

We were definitely engaged though

But encountered?

I’m not sure. (At least not corporately)

And then, almost without thinking, I got in the car, started driving home, and put on the Spurs game.

That little detail bothered me.

It bothered me because of how quickly the moment faded.

One minute, I was in a room filled with worship.  
A few minutes later, I was checking the score.

And I found myself wondering:

**Is this all we mean by worship?**

Not “is this all the artist gave us?”  
Not “is this all the band created?”  
Not “is this all the production achieved?”

But is this all I have learned to expect?

A beautiful room.  
Powerful songs.  
Emotional moments.  
Then the parking lot.  
Then life.

There must be more than this.

Not louder music or bigger moments.

I mean Him.

Jesus.

Because worship is not ultimately about singing—it’s about seeing Him.

And maybe that’s why a room can be full of music yet leave us unchanged.

It’s possible to be moved by worship and still not behold Jesus.

As a worship leader, that thought unsettles me.

We can build great arrangements, transitions, and atmospheres. None of those things are bad. Excellence matters.

But sometimes excellence becomes a curtain—something beautiful in front of something holy.

And if we’re not careful, we admire the curtain and never step through it.

The people who were transformed by Jesus weren’t changed by an event. They saw Him.

And once they did, they couldn’t go back to normal.

That’s what I’m hungry for.

Not worship that’s powerful in the room, but worship that makes Jesus harder to forget in the parking lot.

Worship that follows me into my home, my relationships, my work, and my ordinary life.

Because if I truly encounter Jesus, I don’t just leave with a memory.

I leave with Him.

That’s what David seemed to understand. While religious activity carried on around him, he centered everything around God’s presence.

Maybe that’s the invitation again.

Not to criticize artists, songs, or production.

But to ask:

**Is Jesus actually before us?**

Are we beholding Him, or just admiring what we’ve built around Him?

Maybe the real question after worship isn’t, “Was it good?”

Maybe it’s:

**Did I see Him?**

Did I leave more aware of Jesus than when I arrived?

Did His presence stay with me after the music ended?

I ask because I felt the gap in myself last night.

I left a beautiful worship night, turned on the Spurs game, and realized how quickly I can move on.

So my prayer became simple:

Jesus, I don’t want to just attend worship, enjoy it, or even lead it.

I want to see You.

Because if I see You, worship won’t have to be manufactured.

It will rise naturally.

And if I truly meet You, I won’t just leave saying, “That was amazing.”

I’ll leave changed.

With You. Into the car.

With You. On the drive home.

With You. Into the night.

Into the rest of my life.

See you next Friday.

subject: God as Father Is Not a Metaphor
body:
![](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/56828a12-d631-4f16-9ad8-4585b9695402/ChatGPT_Image_Jun_5__2026__09_28_21_AM.png?t=1780666122)

Last night, I spoke at a young adults group.

At one point I said, “The first title God ever had was Father.”

I meant it.

But even as I said it, I felt how limited that sentence was.

“First” is a time word. It makes us think in terms of beginnings. Before and after. As if there was a moment when God was not Father, and then later He became Father.

But God has no beginning.

There was never a time when God was not.

There was never a time when the Father was not Father, the Son was not Son, or the Spirit was not Spirit.

This is where our words start to fall apart.

How do you speak about the eternal with language trapped inside time?

How do you describe the infinite with sentences that have beginnings and endings?

Still, we try.

Because this matters.

God is love.

But love is not something God started doing after He created us. Love is not God’s response to loneliness. Love did not begin when there was finally someone else around to love.

Before there was a world, before there were people, before there was sin to forgive or pain to heal, God was already love.

Because God was already relationship.

Father. Son. Spirit.

The Father loving the Son.  
The Son receiving and returning that love.  
The Spirit sharing in the eternal communion of love.

That means relationship is not a metaphor God borrowed from us.

It is something we learned from Him.

We often assume we call God Father because we understand human fatherhood.

But what if we have that backwards?

What if fatherhood did not begin on earth and then get projected onto heaven?

What if fatherhood began in God, and every good expression of it on earth is only an echo?

God is not like a father because we understand fatherhood.

Fatherhood exists because God is Father.

Connection exists because God is communion.

Relationship exists because God has never been alone.

That is why we are made for love.

That is why isolation hurts.

That is why belonging feels like oxygen.

We were created by relationship, from relationship, for relationship.

And this is what Jesus came to reveal.

Not merely that God is powerful.

Not merely that God is holy.

Not merely that God can create, command, judge, provide, forgive, and rescue.

All of that is true.

But Jesus came revealing God as Father.

And not Father as a distant religious idea.

Abba.

Near.

Known.

Loved.

Jesus did not call God Father as a comforting metaphor.

He called God Father because He is the Son.

And then He brought us into His own relationship.

He taught us to pray, “Our Father.”

He gave us the Spirit, by whom we cry, “Abba, Father.”

Not as outsiders pretending to be children.

But as sons and daughters brought into the life of the Son.

So maybe Father was not God’s first title.

Maybe that still sounds too small.

Maybe this is better:

Father is God’s eternal name in relationship.

Before God was Creator to creation, He was Father to the Son.

Before He was Redeemer to sinners, He was Son to the Father.

Before He was Comforter to the needy, He was Spirit to the Father.

And now, in Jesus, by the Spirit, we are reminded that He is, and has always been - Father to us.

Not because we earned our way in.

Not because we performed well enough.

But because the Son came to reveal the truth of Our Father with us.

That is the wonder.

The gospel is not God becoming loving.

The gospel is God opening our eyes to the love that has always been.

And somehow, by grace, we are welcomed in.

[The doctrine of the Trinity is as central to Orthodox theology as it is mysterious and mind-boggling. Grace for where I may be wrong. Holy Spirit lead us into all truth. ]  
  
See you next Friday.

subject: The Fire Does Not Come From the Tree
body:
![](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/68a6dabf-3925-4a6a-9bfa-cd0aa986ae9f/ChatGPT_Image_Jun_12__2026__02_52_12_PM.png?t=1781290348)

The other day at worship rehearsal, I felt that familiar tension.

We had just finished practicing, and I could feel a little heaviness in the room. Not rebellion. Not apathy. Just tired people being tired people.

By personality and growing maturity, I am a passionate and expressive worship leader.   
  
I want everyone to be that.   
  
I don't understand why everyone isn't.

And as a worship leader, there’s a part of me that wants to fix that.

Come on, guys. Let’s bring some energy. Let’s be excited. Let’s be alive.

But even as I thought it, I knew that wasn’t quite right.

Because asking people to work up passion is not the same as helping them respond to God.

So I said something like this to the team:

**Let your juice be in the truth.**

Strange phrase. I know.

But what I meant was this:

The fuel for your worship cannot come from the size of the crowd.  
It cannot come from how passionate you feel.  
It cannot come from how “on” you are that day.  
It cannot come from the room giving you something back.

The fuel has to come from Him.

From His presence.  
From His person.  
From the truth of who He is.

That’s what I keep seeing in the burning bush.

Moses sees a bush that is burning, but it is not consumed.

And that detail matters.

The bush got Moses’ attention.

But the bush was not the source of the fire.

It burned, but it was not being eaten alive by the flame.

That is a picture I cannot get away from.

Because so many of us in worship are burning, but we are also being consumed.

We are scraping the bottom of the barrel for passion.  
Trying to work it up.  
Trying to pull more energy out of our tired bodies.  
Trying to manufacture a spiritual intensity we hope will be convincing enough for the room.

And for a while, it can look like fire.

But if the fuel is coming from us, eventually it consumes us.

Our flesh is not a sustainable source for holy fire.

The tree was not feeding the flame.

The fire came from the Fiery One.

And maybe that is the invitation for worship leaders.

Not to become louder.  
Not to become more impressive.  
Not to become professional passion machines.

But to burn with a fire that does not originate in us.

A fire that comes from seeing Him.  
A fire that comes from remembering Him.  
A fire that comes from standing near His presence until response becomes natural again.

Because worship is a response.

It is not hype.  
It is not performance.  
It is not emotional pressure dressed up as spiritual leadership.

It is the heart waking up to truth.

So when I feel tired, flat, distracted, or empty, maybe the answer is not to dig deeper into myself.

Maybe the answer is to turn aside again.

Like Moses did.

To look again.  
To listen again.  
To remember who is in the room.

The goal is not to make the tree burn harder.

The goal is to stand close enough to the Fire.

Because the fuel for our worship was never meant to come from our tree.

It comes from the Fiery One.  
  
See you next Friday

subject: When Did We Give You a Soccer Ball?
body:
![](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/1e6962bf-a1d6-47ba-81cb-a4a9f7caafd5/soccerball.png?t=1781883623)

Last night, my son Jaden came home from a homeless outreach ministry run out of our [church](https://www.theembassy.church/?utm_source=letters.batsirai.com&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=when-did-we-give-you-a-soccer-ball).

Food. Toiletries. Practical things.

Nothing flashy.

But he came home different.

Not proud.

Moved.

The team ended up taking one of the men to Walmart.

That detail stuck with me because Walmart is familiar territory for Jaden. He goes there often for his work. He knows the aisles. The shelves. The normal rhythm of walking in, grabbing what you need, and getting out.

But this time, he walked slowly.

Not as a customer in a hurry.

As a brother beside someone in need.

They helped the man pick out essentials.

Sleeping bags.

Food.

Basic things most of us barely notice.

And then this grown man started marveling at the cereal aisle.

The cereal aisle.

Different boxes. Different kinds. Different choices.

Something so ordinary to us felt like wonder to him.

Then he saw a soccer ball.

And he asked if he could have it.

That was the part that broke Jaden.

Not the sleeping bag.

Not the food.

The soccer ball.

Because buried underneath all the obvious needs was something deeply human.

Not just, “Can I survive?”

But, “Can I play?”

Not just, “Can I make it through the night?”

But, “Can I still have joy?”

A soccer ball.

Small thing.

Huge revelation.

The 2026 World Cup is going on, so maybe it makes sense.

We often think love has to be massive to matter.

Buy someone a house.

Fix their whole life.

Solve every problem.

And yes, big help matters.

But sometimes love looks like toothpaste.

Sometimes it looks like a sleeping bag.

Sometimes it looks like standing in Walmart with someone long enough to notice what makes their face light up.

Sometimes it looks like saying yes to a soccer ball.

Jaden told me that earlier in the evening, while the team was handing out supplies, some of the people receiving them began sharing with others.

They didn’t have much.

But they shared quickly.

Naturally. (Sound familiar?)

Without a committee meeting.

Without a strategy session.

Without needing to be told that generosity was the point.

The people Jaden and the team went to serve were serving too.

That’s the kingdom punch.

You show up thinking you’re bringing Jesus to people.

Then Jesus starts showing up through them.

I personally wasn’t there that night.

I only heard the story when Jaden came home.

But as he talked, I could feel the Lord reframing something in me.

We make church too small.

We think worship is mostly what happens when the band starts.

But if worship is our response to the Lord, then worship was happening in those streets.

It was happening in the bags of food.

It was happening in the shared toiletries.

It was happening in the slow walk through Walmart.

It was happening in the cereal aisle.

It was happening when a man held a soccer ball and remembered joy.

No lights.

No stage.

No setlist.

Still worship.

Street worship.

The kind that smells like kindness.

The kind that doesn’t need a microphone.

The kind that says, “Jesus, I see You here too.”

The kingdom is often hidden in the spectacular.

Sometimes it is more obvious in the simple.

A bag.

A meal.

A blanket.

A ball.

A son coming home with his heart opened wider than when he left.

“This is what I want to do with my life”   
  
That was last night.

And today, on my daughter Simmone’s birthday, I feel the weight of another kind of wealth.

Not the kind you can measure on a statement.

The kind you hear upstairs in the middle of a workday when your kids are singing worship together because they love Jesus.

The kind you see when your daughter is writing songs from a heart that is falling deeper in love with the Lord.

The kind you feel when your son comes home talking about cereal, sleeping bags, generosity, and a soccer ball like he just saw the kingdom with fresh eyes.

That is wealth.

Real wealth.

The kind moth and rust can’t touch.

The kind no market can crash.

The kind that makes you stop and whisper, “Lord, we are blessed.”

Not because life is perfect.

Not because we have everything.

But because Jesus is forming love in our house.

And love is starting to look practical.

Love is starting to leave the building.

Love is starting to walk the aisles of Walmart.

Yes, sometimes, love sings a song.

And sometimes, love buys a soccer ball.

See you next Friday

For when you saw me hungry, you fed me. When you found me thirsty, you gave me drink. When I had no place to stay, you invited me in, and when I was poorly clothed, you covered me. When I was sick, you tenderly cared for me, and when I was in prison you visited me.’

“Then the godly will answer him, ‘Lord, **when did we see you hungry** or thirsty and give you food and something to drink? When did we see you with no place to stay and invite you in? When did we see you poorly clothed and cover you? When did we see you sick and tenderly care for you, or in prison and visit you?’

“And the King will answer them, ‘Don’t you know? When you cared for one of the least of these, my little ones, my true brothers and sisters, you demonstrated love for me.’

 Matthew 25:35–40 TPT.

subject: I Thought I Was Chasing Too Many Rabbits
body:
![](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/774dd5c9-8fc6-41f5-8d33-faefaf313f5d/CleanShot_2026-02-20_at_14.30.05.png?t=1771616021)

I’ve done almost everything I can do to finish building [*Already Loved*](http://alreadylovedkids.com?utm_source=letters.batsirai.com&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=i-thought-i-was-chasing-too-many-rabbits).

The book is made.  
The product is built.  
The tweaks are mostly excuses now.

Which means the next step is obvious:

Talk about it.

And that’s where I froze.

Not because I don’t believe in it.

I do.

But because putting something out there means it can be ignored.  
Misunderstood.  
Rejected.

So instead of marketing, I started spiraling.

*What am I even about?*

Worship?  
Parenting?  
Tech?  
AI?  
Books?

My dad always talks about “chasing too many rabbits.”

And I wondered if that was me.

Because if I’m not about worship anymore…  
what were the last 30 years of my life about?

Then it hit me.

I am still about worship.

But worship for me was never just music.

It was about facilitating an encounter.

And encounter is about connection.

Connection with God.  
Connection with people.  
Connection with who we really are.

That’s what *Already Loved* is too.

A worship song helps people hear the Father’s heart.

This book helps a child hear the Father’s heart through a parent’s voice.

Different tool.  
Same mission.

Connection.

And maybe that’s why this message matters so much to me.

Because some of the deepest shame in my story came from becoming pregnant in Bible college.

For years, that felt like the part to hide.

The disqualifying part.

The part I never wanted to build anything on.

But God loves doing this.

He takes what shame tried to bury  
and turns it into testimony.

He loves airing our dirty laundry… in the sunshine, because sunshine is the best disinfectant… and people can learn and benefit from what they see.

He turns things around for our good.

The cross was meant to be shameful.  
God made it THE victory.

The water at Cana was for washing.  
Jesus made it wine. Amazing wine.

And now I’m beginning to see:

Maybe *Already Loved* isn’t a side project.

Maybe it’s the banner.

Before you lead worship, you are already loved.  
Before you parent well, you are already loved.  
Before you launch the thing, you are already loved.  
Before your story makes sense, you are already loved.

That’s the message.

That’s the work.

That’s the one rabbit.

And if I spend my life helping people believe they are loved by God the way the Father loves Jesus…

That will be enough.

You are already loved.   
  
Next week, the newsletter will be coming from [iamalreadyloved.com](http://iamalreadyloved.com?utm_source=letters.batsirai.com&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=i-thought-i-was-chasing-too-many-rabbits)

subject: My Gift Made Room for Me
body:
![](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/f55c2f55-6872-43fe-87c0-d5d649ad6298/homecoming_king.jpg?t=1783108693)

University of Western Ontario, Homecoming King 1995… yep.   
(found out a year later she had a crush on me!)

I learned early how to be loved.

Sing.

That was the formula.

I was okay at sports. Decent at school. But when I sang, people’s faces changed.

They leaned in.

They smiled.

They remembered my name.

My gift made room for me. Proverbs 18:16

At the University of Western Ontario (one of the biggest in Canada), I competed for Homecoming King. I had come from Zimbabwe into one of the largest university residences in North America — surrounded by athletes, confident people, beautiful people, smart people.

So I did what I knew worked.

I sang “A Whole New World” by Peabo Bryson and Regina Belle.

And it worked.

I won. Everything…

There’s a picture somewhere of me as Homecoming King — crowned, smiling, celebrated, seen.

And that moment reinforced in me something enticing...

But also dangerous.

Something I had learned years before

Your voice makes things happen.

**This is how you get loved.**

Be impressive.  
Be talented.  
Be useful.  
Be excellent.  
Be memorable.

Get through the door.

Then maybe you’ll belong.

But here’s the problem.

The thing that makes room for you can become the thing you think makes you lovable.

For me, it was music.

For someone else, it might be beauty.  
Intelligence.  
Humor.  
Money.  
Spirituality.  
Strength.  
Success.  
Being needed.  
Being low-maintenance.  
Being the one who “doesn’t care.”

We all find a way to answer the same question:

**What must I do to be loved?**

But a newborn child never asks that.

He does not perform for his father.

He does not prove his worth.

He does not sing on key.

He simply exists.

And the father’s love is already turned toward him.

That is the truth I keep forgetting.

God did not start loving me when I found my gift.

He loved me before I found the room.

Before the stage.  
Before the applause.  
Before the crown.  
Before anyone knew my name.

My gift made room for me.

But it did not make me loved.

I already was.

And so are you.

See you next Friday.

subject: I am because He is
previewText: I am afraid - but He's not.
body:
This is late; I’m sorry, but I'm trying something new… video and a post. You can watch, read, or both.

[AlreadyLoved](http://alreadylovedkids.com?utm_source=letters.batsirai.com&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=i-am-because-he-is) is ready for the preschooler or mom in your life.

The product exists. The app is live. People can actually use it.

And yet I keep finding things to improve.

A sentence could be clearer. A screen could look better. The experience could be smoother. There is always one more adjustment I can make before I put it in front of people.

Some of that is care.

But if I’m honest, some of it is hiding.

Improvement had become camouflage.

Because the real work now is not inside the product. The real work is walking into the marketplace and saying:

**Here. I made this.**

And that sentence feels strangely vulnerable.

Because the moment I share it, people can reject it.

They can ignore it.

They can decide I’m not interesting enough, articulate enough, polished enough, or credible enough to listen to.

So I have collected a million reasons not to begin.

I am not eloquent enough.

I am not cool-looking enough.

I am not good on camera.

I do not have the right studio.

I am not equipped for this.

A million little **“I am nots.”**

Which is almost funny, because the entire book is about identity.

I built something to help children know who they are, while quietly believing that I am not enough to tell anyone about it.

This week, I found myself thinking about Moses.

God appears to him and calls him to lead Israel. Moses immediately begins explaining why He has chosen the wrong person.

Who am I?

What if they don’t believe me?

I’m not a good speaker.

Moses keeps saying, **“I am not.”**

And God reveals Himself as **“I AM.”**

Moses keeps referencing his limitations.

God keeps referencing His presence.

That is what strikes me about the name God gives Moses: “I AM WHO I AM.”

God does not look outside Himself for a definition. He has no external reference point. He is the anchor beneath every other reality.

God says:

**I am because I am.**

But I am created. I am not self-defined.

So perhaps my confession is:

**I am because He is.**

An apple seed does not determine what it is by examining how much fruit it has produced.

Before the first apple appears, the seed already carries its identity.

Its origin tells you what it is.

But I keep looking at my output to determine my identity.

How well did I speak?

How many people responded?

Did the video look professional?

Did anyone download the app?

Was I impressive enough?

I turn fruit into identity.

And when the fruit does not look the way I hoped, I begin telling myself stories about who I am.

I am not gifted.

I am not capable.

I am not wanted.

I am not enough.

Those stories may feel true.

But feelings are not always reliable witnesses.

So I’m beginning to ask a different question:

**Who told me that?**

Who decided that I needed an impressive studio before I could speak about love?

Who said I needed to look cooler before I could tell children who they are?

Who said eloquence was the qualification for obedience?

It wasn’t God.

The Father’s word over Jesus was not based on an impressive public result.

Before the miracles, before the crowds, and before the cross, the Father said:

**“You are my beloved Son. In you I am well pleased.”**

Origin before output.

Beloved before achievement.

Identity before fruit.

That is the message at the centre of Already Loved.

And apparently, it is not just a message I am meant to teach.

It is one I need to believe.

I do not need to become impressive enough to share what I have made.

I do not need to eliminate every “I am not” before I obey.

Moses brought God his inadequacy.

God answered with His presence.

So perhaps this is my next step:

Not another adjustment.

Not another excuse disguised as excellence.

Just the courage to walk into the marketplace and say:

**Here. I made this.**

Not because I am everything I think I need to be.

But because **I am because He is.**

subject: The Fear of Being Seen
previewText: has nothing to do with the solution..
body:
![](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/4297474b-5ab7-4d1a-9f02-21123613fa5a/ChatGPT_Image_Jul_17__2026__05_40_00_PM.png?t=1784324448)

A few nights ago, I was getting ready for bed when I asked the Lord a question:

**Why am I still afraid?**

Why do I feel this inner resistance whenever I think about promoting Already Loved?

Why does turning on a camera and talking about the thing that matters most to me feel so difficult?

His answer came almost immediately:

**Because you’re afraid of people.**

Not really afraid of the subject.

Afraid of what people might think about me.

There is something about standing in public and saying, *Here I am. This is what I believe. This is what I’ve made. This matters to me.*

It feels like drawing attention to myself.

It isn’t only Already Loved. I’ve felt it with worship too. Any time I create something and place it in front of people, the same resistance rises.

What will they think?

Will they misunderstand me?

Will they think I’m trying too hard?

Will they reject the thing—or, worse, reject me?

Last week, I recorded a video.

That was a real step for me. I included it in my newsletter and uploaded it to YouTube.

But I didn’t make clips.

I didn’t share it on social media.

I didn’t really tell anyone it was there.

I had technically made myself visible, but I had placed the video in one of the safest rooms I could find: a YouTube page with almost no one watching.

I could say, “Well, I posted it.”

And I did.

But I was still hiding.

As I sat with this, an image came to me.

Imagine that you are drowning in the ocean.

You don’t know how much longer you can keep your head above the water. Then a lifeboat appears. Someone throws you a life preserver and reaches out to pull you in.

In that moment, it doesn’t matter how you ended up in the ocean.

Maybe you fell from a plane.

Maybe your boat capsized.

Maybe you swam too far from shore.

Maybe you ignored every warning and jumped in yourself.

There may be a real explanation. There may be a long story behind it.

But while you are treading water, understanding the story will not rescue you.

You don’t need a perfect explanation.

You need to grab the life preserver.

I have spent a lot of time trying to understand my fear.

Where did it come from?

Why do I hide?

What happened to me?

Why is visibility so hard?

Those can be worthwhile questions. But I think I quietly began believing that once I finally understood my fear, I would be free from it.

As though the explanation itself could pull me out of the water.

It can’t.

Freedom does not always begin with finally understanding why I am afraid.

Sometimes freedom begins by taking hold of the One who has already come for me.

It made me think about Adam and Eve.

They had walked with God in the garden. They knew the sound of His presence. But after shame entered their story, they heard Him coming and hid.

God called out:

“Where are you?”

He wasn’t asking because He had lost them.

He was inviting them to come out of hiding.

I wonder what might have happened if they had stepped forward and simply said:

**Here I am. I don’t know what to do.**

Instead, shame told them to stay hidden until they could explain themselves, cover themselves or somehow repair what had happened.

I recognize that instinct.

I keep thinking I need to become more confident before I show up.

I need to resolve the fear.

I need to be certain that people will understand.

I need to feel safe before I can say, “Here I am.”

But perhaps confidence is not something I must manufacture before coming into the light.

Perhaps it is something I receive in His presence.

Peace is easier there.

Joy is easier there.

Freedom is easier there.

Even courage is easier there.

The answer is not to stand in the ocean and analyze the water.

The answer is to let myself be rescued.

To stop hiding.

To take the next small step into visibility, even with fear still present.

Last week, that step was recording the video.

This week, perhaps it is sharing it where people can actually see it.

Not because I have conquered every fear.

Not because I no longer care what anyone thinks.

But because Someone is already in the boat, reaching toward me.

The question may not be:

**Why am I still afraid?**

The question may simply be:

**Will I come?**

Will I leave the hiding place?

Will I take hold of the hand that is already reaching for me?

Will I answer the voice calling through the garden?

**Here I am.**

subject: Who Told You That?
body:
![](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/dd2e9066-fa2b-4621-aed1-2fa65bdfee21/ChatGPT_Image_Jul_24__2026__04_55_14_PM.png?t=1784926554)

### **(Watch the short video** 👆**)**

My teacher didn’t make me smarter that night.

She didn’t teach me a new formula.

She didn’t give me a better study plan.

She changed the story I believed about myself.

That was enough.

For most of that year, I had been collecting evidence:

No A’s.

Other students answering faster.

Me feeling like I was barely keeping up.

The evidence became a conclusion.

The conclusion became a belief.

And eventually, the belief started sounding like my identity.

Not:

*I haven’t received an A yet.*

But:

*I’m not an A student.*

That is how identity lies usually work.

They take something that happened…

and turn it into something you are.

You failed.

So you’re a failure.

You were rejected.

So you’re unwanted.

You made a mistake.

So you ruin everything.

Someone didn’t love you well.

So you must be difficult to love.

An experience becomes an interpretation.

The interpretation becomes a belief.

And the belief starts introducing itself as you.

Then someone you trust says one sentence:

“No. That isn’t who you are.”

And suddenly, the story begins to crack.

My teacher didn’t give me intelligence.

She saw something that fear had been hiding.

For one night, I trusted her assessment more than my own.

I stopped trying to prove that I belonged in the class.

I rested as though I already did.

And the next morning, my performance caught up with what she had already seen.

That is why God’s question in the garden is so powerful.

Adam and Eve were hiding.

They were ashamed.

They were seeing themselves differently.

God asked:

**“Who told you that?”**

Not just:

“What did you do?”

But:

Whose voice taught you to see yourself this way?

Who told you that your failure had become your name?

Who told you that your weakness disqualified you from love?

Who told you that God was disappointed, distant or waiting for you to become better before coming close?

We rarely question these voices.

We just repeat them.

*I’m too much.*

*I’m not enough.*

*I’m behind.*

*I’m bad with money.*

*I’m not a leader.*

*I’m not creative.*

*I always mess things up.*

But repetition doesn’t make something true.

It only makes it familiar.

And familiar lies can feel more believable than unfamiliar truth.

Here is the truth:

You are not defined by the worst thing you have done.

You are not defined by the worst thing someone did to you.

You are not defined by your current performance.

You are defined by the One who made you.

Before Jesus performed a miracle, preached a sermon or proved anything, the Father called Him beloved.

Beloved wasn’t the reward.

Beloved was the starting point.

And that is where transformation begins for us too.

Not by trying harder to become worthy of love.

But by learning to live from the truth that, in Christ, we already are.

Maybe you don’t need another hour of striving.

Maybe you need to question the story that keeps making you strive.

Who told you that you weren’t smart enough?

Good enough?

Worthy enough?

Loved enough?

And who gave them the authority to name you?

subject: Lay Down Your Oars
body:
![](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/0abfb4e1-b0e6-49af-9d88-b0cb56ae4126/ChatGPT_Image_Jul_31__2026__05_33_27_PM.png?t=1785533629)

This week, I heard a phrase I haven’t been able to shake:

**Lay down your oars and raise your sail.**

It found me at the right time.

I had been working on Already Loved—trying to figure out how to market it, explain it and make people care.

What should I say?

What is my personal brand?

How do I make this interesting?

Should I be funnier?

How do I do YouTube?

How do I do all the other things everyone says I need to do?

My mind was moving in a hundred directions, but somehow I wasn’t getting anywhere.

I was rowing furiously in one place.

And I sensed the Lord saying:

## **Lay down your oars.**

The oars were my self-effort. The sweat, strain and need to manufacture an outcome. The belief that if I could just work harder, think faster or find the perfect strategy, I could force the boat forward.

But a sailboat doesn’t move because the sailor tries harder.

No amount of huffing and puffing can make the wind blow.

The sailor raises the sail.

Then waits.

That feels vulnerable.

Because raising the sail means admitting:

*Lord, this depends on You.*

This company. This project. This dream I care so much about.

I can build the boat. I can prepare the sail. I can listen and respond when You speak.

But I cannot create the wind.

That kind of dependence is uncomfortable in a culture that tells us to hustle, grind and make our own way.

We like oars because they give us the illusion of control.

Even if we are exhausted, at least we can say we are doing something.

The disciples had been fishing all night. Working, sweating and throwing their nets into the water again and again.

Nothing.

Then Jesus told them to put the net on the other side of the boat.

A boat isn’t that wide.

How could there be no fish on one side and more than they could carry on the other?

It didn’t make much sense.

But they listened.

And the fish came.

I don’t know what “the other side of the boat” looks like for me yet.

I don’t know how God will bring the right people to Already Loved or how He will make the fish jump into the net.

But I’m beginning to see that the fish may not even be the point.

The point is doing this **with Him**.

Moses understood that.

When God promised to lead Israel towards a land flowing with milk and honey, Moses essentially said, “We’re not going anywhere unless You come with us.”

He didn’t just want the destination.

He wanted God.

Because what is the Promised Land without His presence?

What is success if I arrive there alone, exhausted from rowing?

I have a phrase that may sound almost heretical:

### **Heaven would be hell without Him.**

Because heaven is heaven wherever He is.

You could argue that while Israel was still walking through the wilderness—following the cloud by day and the fire by night—they had already found the promise.

God was with them.

Emmanuel.

What more could they want?

A few weeks ago, Pastor Paul spoke at our church about Sabbath.

He said Sabbath is a day when we trust that, even while we stop working, God continues holding everything together.

The train will not fall off the tracks because I took my hands off it.

That is rest.

Not inactivity. Trust.

Raising the sail doesn’t mean I do nothing.

The disciples still had to move the net.

The sailor still watches the wind, adjusts the ropes and steers the boat.

But the power moving everything forward comes from somewhere else.

So I’m learning to pray:

*Lord, I have the boat.*

*I have the sail.*

*I will do what You ask me to do.*

*But You provide the wind.*

*Take me wherever You want to go.*

And if the destination does not include You, I don’t want it.

So when they tell you that everything depends on you…

When they tell you to work harder, hustle more and force your own way forward…

Pause and ask:

### **Who told you that?**

It wasn’t your Dad.

See you next Friday

subject: "I dont want to be black"
previewText: What Must I Become to Be Loved?
body:
![](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/39e7405f-2050-4a3b-a764-465a00a3623d/be-black.png?t=1786131888)

I watched a video this week that caught me off guard.

A little Black girl, maybe five or six years old, is crying.

She tells her mom:

**“I don’t want to be Black.”**

Her mom responds beautifully.

She reminds her how beautiful she is. How beautiful it is to be Black. That God made her the way she is for a reason.

Then she pulls her close.

They hug.

And honestly, it sounds like the right response.

But I paused the video there because something else was bothering me.

This is absolutely a story about race.

But I think underneath the racial wound is an even older question:

**Do I belong?**

Because when that little girl says, “I want to be white,” she isn’t only making a statement about skin colour.

Somewhere, somehow, she has begun connecting *being different* with *being outside*.

And once that lie takes root, another one follows quickly:

**I need to become something else in order to belong.**

That one hit me.

Because I’ve believed versions of it too.

Not about my skin.

But in friend groups. In culture. In rooms where I quietly wondered which version of myself would be easiest to accept.

Maybe I should talk differently.

Like different things.

Tone this part of me down.

Turn that part up.

We learn to edit ourselves before anyone ever explicitly asks us to.

And underneath all of it is basically the same question:

**What must I do to be loved?**

That little girl’s answer, in that moment, was:

*Maybe I need to become someone else.*

Ours can be more sophisticated.

Maybe I need to achieve more.

Be funnier.

Be more successful.

Be less awkward.

Be more spiritual.

Get invited.

Wear the right thing.

Sit at the right table.

Prove that I deserve to be here.

Different fruit.

Same root.

**I don’t believe that I already belong.**

And this is where beloved identity changes the way I see behaviour.

Because behaviour is often the visible fruit of an invisible belief.

Before I only ask, *How do we correct what someone is doing?*

I’m beginning to wonder:

**What are they believing for this behaviour to make sense?**

What lie would have to be true?

Maybe the better question isn’t simply:

“Why would you want to be someone else?”

Maybe somewhere underneath it is:

**Who told you that who you are isn’t enough to belong?**

Who told you love was waiting on the other side of becoming?

Who told you acceptance had prerequisites?

Who told you that you had to earn your place at the table?

Because the Gospel begins somewhere completely different.

Not with what we must become to finally be loved.

But with Love coming toward us first.

Before the performance.

Before the improvement.

Before we figured ourselves out.

Before we could make ourselves acceptable.

**Already loved.**

Maybe so much of transformation begins there.

Not helping people become worthy of belonging.

But helping them discover they never had to become someone else to be welcomed in the first place.

And when the old lie whispers,

*You need to become something else before you can be loved…*

I keep hearing another question:

**Who told you that?**  
  
See you next Friday

subject: You Can’t Bribe a Seed
body:
![](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/d9ec077f-4c56-49e4-8902-f7f3c0f7d8b2/47bb9820-64c1-4033-bd58-22b6e640ef73.png?t=1786731435)

I was talking with a pastor friend earlier today about growing a young adults ministry.

It reminded me of one we inherited years ago.

At one point, the young adults ministry at our church had been huge. Hundreds of people. Vibrant. Exciting.

By the time Aimee and I were asked to help, most of that was gone.

What remained was maybe 10 or 15 people.

And honestly, they weren't necessarily the people someone would have picked if the goal was to rebuild something impressive.

But they were there.

So we started there.

There was a large room available to us, but we didn't use it.

Ten people spread across a big room somehow feels like failure.

Instead, we met in this little side prayer room. There were couches. We pulled some chairs around them. It felt more like somebody's living room than a church service.

And we started doing life together.

People came to our house. We ate together. Painted walls together. Talked. Prayed.

I used to say I wanted people to have refrigerator rights in our home.

As in: don't knock politely and wait to be served. Come in, open the fridge and grab something.

That kind of relationship.

Eventually those people started inviting other people.

Then the little room became too small.

So we moved into the bigger room.

And then more people came.

Looking back, I think I understand something now that I didn't have language for then.

We weren't trying to grow fruit.

We were growing roots.

And there's a difference.

We are obsessed with fruit.

How many people came?

How much did it grow?

How much did you sell?

How many people watched?

Did it work?

Where are the results?

And when the fruit doesn't appear quickly enough, the temptation is to manufacture some.

Staple an apple onto the branch.

Paint it red.

Stand back and say, “Look! Growth!”

And for a while, it might even look convincing.

Until somebody bites into it.

Or a storm comes.

I've done versions of this more times than I'd like to admit.

Trying to make something look like the thing I believe it could someday become.

But God doesn't seem nearly as embarrassed by seeds as I am.

A seed can become a redwood.

But I can't bribe it into becoming one tomorrow.

I can give it good soil.

I can water it.

I can protect it.

I can make sure it gets light.

But there are some parts of growth I simply cannot do.

And maybe that's the point.

When a seed first begins to grow, we don't put it in the middle of a field and yell:

“YOU'RE AN OAK TREE. ACT LIKE IT.”

We put it in a tiny cup.

Not because we've lowered our expectations for it.

Because we understand what it is.

That little cup isn't an insult to the oak.

It's protection.

There will come a day when the cup is much too small.

But today, it might be exactly what the tree needs.

I wonder how many times I've despised the little cup because I was comparing my seedling to somebody else's 50-year-old tree.

Their branches.

Their shade.

Their fruit.

Without seeing the decades of roots underneath it.

Jesus seemed remarkably comfortable with seeds.

Mustard seeds.

Wheat.

Vines.

Branches.

Fruit.

Things disappearing underground before anyone could see what was happening.

Maybe because the Kingdom has always been more comfortable with hidden growth than we are.

We keep asking:

Where's the fruit?

And maybe God is looking underground saying:

Look at those roots.

Because fruit has seasons.

Leaves have seasons.

There are moments when a healthy tree can look almost dead.

But winter isn't failure.

And spring can't be rushed.

The work is knowing what season you're in.

If it's planting season, plant.

If it's rooting season, protect the roots.

If it's pruning season, prune.

And when fruit finally comes, receive it.

But don't staple fruit onto a sapling because you're ashamed that it isn't an oak tree yet.

I've been thinking about this in more than ministry lately.

My work.

My family.

Already Loved.

Even my own life with God.

I'm beginning to wonder whether maturity looks less like becoming really good at producing outcomes...

and more like becoming comfortable tending what God has actually put in front of me.

This seed.

These people.

This little room.

This season.

And trusting that the One who put an oak inside an acorn knows how to get it out.

Maybe my job was never to make the tree grow.

Maybe my job is simply to tend the soil.

And let God be God.  
  
See you next Friday

subject: You Don’t Really Want to Know Your Purpose
previewText: Purpose is easy once you know this...
body:
![](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/40ffcfb7-4b8f-4e3f-885e-fbeef7cb8bf1/3AE1C807-D203-4599-A943-F7AAAC60EF5B.png?t=1787347077)

**(sorry, no video this week)**

I must have been eleven or twelve.

I was lip-syncing a Beatles song in a school talent show. There was a moment in the song when someone laughed, so I threw my head back and gave the biggest, most dramatic fake laugh I could.

The room erupted.

They weren’t laughing at me. They were enjoying me.

I remember thinking, *Oh my gosh. I can move a room.*

For years, I called that purpose.

Entertainment became music. Music became worship leading. The stage changed, but the conviction remained: *This is what I’m here to do.*

But I’m beginning to wonder if my search for purpose was really a search for identity.

We ask:

*What am I supposed to do with my life?*

But underneath that question, we may be asking:

*Who am I? Do I matter? Is there a reason I’m here?*

Purpose becomes a proxy for identity.

We hope that if we can discover the right assignment, we’ll finally know our value. So when someone asks who we are, we answer with what we do:

“I’m a doctor.”

“I’m a parent.”

“I’m a worship leader.”

Purpose matters—but it is secondary.

An apple seed doesn’t discover what it is by deciding what fruit to produce. It produces apples because it came from an apple.

Its identity comes from its origin.

Its fruit is the byproduct.

The same is true of Jesus.

Before He preached, healed anyone or went to the cross, the Father said:

*You are My beloved Son.*

The Father answered the identity question before Jesus began His public work.

Jesus didn’t do those things to become the Son. He did them because He was the Son.

What He did flowed from who He was.

So perhaps the first question isn’t:

*What am I here to do?*

Perhaps it is:

*Who am I—and who told me?*

That school audience told me I could move a room. But the same room could have changed its mind the moment I stopped entertaining it.

Conditional sources give us conditional identities.

The Father’s voice is different.

He speaks before the performance.

Purpose is not the path to identity. Purpose is what grows when identity takes root.

I still love moving a room. I still love leading worship.

But the room no longer gets to name me.

**see you next Friday**.

subject: I ran out of breath leading worship
body:
![](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/76fc8bc0-4840-4434-8703-d93fceaf6891/B687A7BC-90DD-4C00-BB9D-35BD808BE8DC.PNG?t=1787941068)

I lead worship with a lot of energy.

Maybe it’s the African in me. Maybe it’s the extrovert. Maybe it’s the performer. Whatever it is, standing still has never really been my thing.

I love leading with my whole body.

But sometimes, halfway through a song on Sunday, I feel myself getting tired.

I pull back from the microphone. Take a breath. Try to recover before leading the next song.

Sometimes I think about artists who tour for months, performing two-hour shows several nights a week.

The physical endurance required is incredible.

As much as I would love to tour someday, I’ve had to ask myself an uncomfortable question:

Could my body actually do it?

I don’t mean whether I have the voice, the songs, or the calling.

Could I physically sustain it?

That question led me back to something Paul wrote:

“Offer your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God—this is your true and proper worship.”

I’ve heard that verse countless times.

But I’m not sure I’ve always heard the word *bodies*.

I think I quietly translated it into something more spiritual:

Offer God your heart.

Offer Him your desires.

Don’t use your body to sin.

All true.

But Paul doesn’t tell us only to offer God our invisible parts. He tells us to offer our bodies.

Our actual bodies.

The bodies that breathe, sleep, eat, move, ache, age, become exhausted, and occasionally run out of breath in the middle of a song.

I used to think my body was simply the instrument I used to worship.

Now I’m wondering if my body is also part of the worship I offer.

That doesn’t mean physical fitness determines whether someone is qualified to lead worship. Thinness isn’t holiness. Health and appearance can become idols just as easily as comfort can.

Our bodies also carry histories, illnesses, limitations, genetics, medications, grief, and circumstances that cannot be reduced to discipline or a number on a scale.

But avoiding shame cannot mean avoiding the question altogether.

If my body belongs to God, then how I care for it cannot be completely disconnected from my worship.

What if going for a walk is worship?

What if lifting weights is worship?

What if going for a run, eating the salad, or putting down the second helping of dessert can become an offering to God?

Not simply because I want to look better.

Not because healthier people are more holy.

Not because God loves me more when I make the “right” choice.

Romans 12 begins somewhere much safer than that:

❝

“In view of God’s mercy…”

 Romans 12:1 

The offering is a response to mercy—not an attempt to earn it.

Shame says, “Your body makes you unacceptable.”

Worship says, “Because you are already accepted, your body matters.”

Of course, a salad isn’t automatically more spiritual than dessert.

Sometimes receiving dessert with gratitude may be worship.

Sometimes putting it down may be worship.

Sometimes worship looks like movement.

Sometimes it looks like rest.

Sometimes it looks like enjoying what God has given me.

Sometimes it looks like telling an appetite, “You don’t get to lead me.”

The action alone isn’t what makes it worship.

It’s the offering.

It’s taking an ordinary physical choice and saying:

“God, this body is Yours too.”

Maybe worship is much more physical than I have allowed it to be.

Maybe the walk counts.

Maybe the weights count.

Maybe the decision nobody sees—made in a kitchen, nowhere near a microphone—can be as much an offering as the song I lead on Sunday.

Because perhaps my body isn’t merely the instrument through which I worship.

My body is (a big 😂) part of the worship I bring.

subject: The Gift Was Never Addressed to Me
body:
![](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/5458ec2b-4a3f-493b-aaa7-dfdbf60f338d/gift_for_dad.png?t=1788538414)

It was late last night when my daughter walked through the door after a worship concert.

I had bought her the tickets, so I stayed up long enough to ask the obvious question:

“How was it?”

Her face lit up.

She told me about the lights, the energy and the way they mixed pop music with worship. She is an artist herself. She wants to make music, but she also loves leading worship. That night, she saw those two parts of herself occupying the same stage.

“You could tell he wanted to be a pop star,” she said, “but now he’s leading worship.”

She meant it positively.

Here was someone bringing all of that creativity, energy and showmanship into an expression of worship. It showed her that Christians could love Jesus and have fun. Worship didn’t have to fit neatly inside the usual Sunday-morning box.

I understood exactly what she meant.

But I could also imagine someone else walking into the same room and being appalled.

Too many lights.

Too much energy.

Too much attention on the person leading.

*He clearly wants to be a star.*

It is easy to look at someone else’s expression and decide that we know what is happening in their heart.

Perhaps that unsettled me because I have asked the same questions about myself.

I lead worship with a lot of energy. I move. I get loud. I sing with my whole body. Maybe it’s the African in me. Maybe it’s the extrovert. Maybe it’s the performer.

It’s simply how I respond.

But sometimes I wonder:

*Am I drawing too much attention to myself?*

*Should I tone it down?*

*Should I dim my light so people can see Jesus?*

Those are worthwhile questions. Anyone standing on a stage should remain honest about what is happening inside them.

But I’m beginning to see how quickly honest reflection can become judgment—both of ourselves and of others.

We measure worship by what we know.

In a charismatic church, silence can feel like something is missing. In a quieter tradition, singing the same chorus for twenty minutes might feel excessive. One room has stained glass and stillness. Another has smoke machines and subwoofers.

Every tradition has its own liturgy, even the churches that insist they don’t have one.

And somehow, our familiar pattern becomes the pattern we believe God prefers.

That night, talking with my daughter, I started thinking about gifts.

If someone gave me a vacuum cleaner for Christmas, I might wonder what I had done to offend them. Someone else might open a Dyson and lose their mind with joy.

One person wants an iPad. Another would trade it immediately for a weekend hiking trip.

The people watching cannot determine the value of the gift.

Only the recipient can.

And often, what makes the gift meaningful isn’t the object itself. It is the intimacy between the giver and the receiver.

*You know me.*

*You noticed.*

*You remembered what matters to me.*

That is what makes the woman with the perfume so striking.

She poured something expensive over Jesus, and the people watching immediately reviewed her offering.

*What a waste.*

*That money could have been used for something better.*

They saw irresponsibility. Jesus received love.

The difference was not in the perfume.

It was in who was evaluating the gift.

I wonder how often we stand beside someone else’s offering and behave as though it was addressed to us.

We call it too loud.

Too quiet.

Too emotional.

Too restrained.

Too rehearsed.

Too spontaneous.

Too Catholic.

Too charismatic.

Too much like a concert.

Too much like a funeral.

But the gift was never addressed to us.

That doesn’t mean every expression automatically pleases God. Scripture gives us offerings that were received and offerings that were not. Abel offered by faith. David refused to give God something that cost him nothing.

The heart still matters.

Truth still matters.

What we offer still matters.

But the form alone cannot reveal the heart behind it.

Expression is a vehicle. Culture helps give that vehicle its shape. The deeper substance is our response to who God has revealed Himself to be.

When Jesus spoke with the Samaritan woman, the argument was about the correct place to worship.

This mountain or Jerusalem?

Jesus moved the conversation beyond both locations. The Father is seeking people who will worship in spirit and truth.

He is not merely seeking worship.

He is seeking worshippers.

People who know Him and respond to Him.

People whose offering grows out of relationship rather than religious obligation.

So perhaps the most important question is not whether worship looks right, sounds right or feels familiar.

Perhaps it is:

***Father, did this come from knowing You?***

*Was I responding to what I have seen of You—or simply repeating what I have always done?*

*Did I bring You my heart, or only the worship culture that taught me how to look like I did?*   
  
(gulp)

I’m tying to become slower at reviewing other people’s gifts.

After all, I’m standing beside the altar.

I’m not the One receiving them.  
  
see you next Friday

subject: Start with Who
body:
![](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/0f2176aa-b11c-4b11-bf09-ed3ec08a8dcc/45AF0E16-958C-4C5E-BD66-AF1E8930875E.png?t=1789153481)

For most of the past year, I’ve been trying to find the right words.

I’m building AlreadyLoved, a personalized children’s book that helps parents speak God’s love into their child’s life. And I kept working on how to explain it.

The headline. The pain point. The thing that would make a parent say, “Yes. That’s what I want.”

Somewhere in all that marketing work, a simple sentence finally surfaced:

“I want my child to know God for themselves.”

And I recognized it.

That’s what I’ve wanted all these years leading worship, too.

Different setting. Same desire.

Whether I’m holding a microphone or helping a parent open a book at bedtime, I want to help someone know Him.

Not just know what to say about Him.

Know Him.

We can surround our children with Christian things.

Bible stories. Songs. Shows. Memory verses. Church every Sunday.

I’m grateful for those things. But I wonder if we sometimes mistake a child’s ability to repeat what we’ve taught them for a relationship with the One we’re teaching them about.

And honestly, I wonder that about myself.

I can know the songs. Explain the lyrics. Lead the room.

And still get so occupied with what we’re doing that I lose sight of who we’re with.

That’s why encounter matters so much to me.

Not because every service needs a dramatic moment. But because there’s a difference between discussing someone’s love and becoming aware that they love *you*.

The God I’ve heard about becomes personal.

His kindness has something to do with my actual life. My fear. The thing I’m ashamed of. The question I haven’t said out loud.

And once you’ve tasted that, doing religious things just for the sake of doing them isn’t enough anymore.

You want Him.

For a child, that might begin with something very ordinary.

Someone was cruel at school.

They’re afraid in the dark.

They lied, and now they don’t know what happens next.

Knowing that God helped David matters. But so does discovering: *He is with me when I’m afraid, too.*

Not just, “God is loving.”

But, “Can I come to Him after what I just did?”

That’s where what we teach about God meets the life our child is actually living.

And it starts with who.

Who is this God? What is He like? How does He see me?

As they come to know who He is, they begin to understand who they are in His love.

That’s what I mean by identity-first parenting.

And I’m realizing it’s what I mean by worship, too.

Before, “What song should we sing?”

*Who are we singing to?*

Before, “How do I get everyone to engage?”

*Who are these people He loves, and how can I help them notice Him?*

The practical questions still matter. But they make more sense when I remember who they’re for.

I thought I was trying to explain a book.

I think I was remembering what I’m here for.

I want to help people know God for themselves. The God revealed in Jesus. Not just inherit someone else’s words about Him, but find themselves addressed by His love.

I can’t manufacture that encounter. A parent can’t either. There isn’t a book or a song that guarantees it.

But we can make room. We can tell the stories, welcome the questions, pray together, and live in ways that help His love become recognizable.

I keep coming back to this picture of being a doorkeeper in the house of the Lord.

There’s something about that I love.

After all my work trying to find the right words, perhaps the words I’ve been reaching for are simpler than I thought:

“Come in. I want you to meet Him.”

See you next Friday

subject: Your lap is their first chapel.
previewText: Your child needs to know WHO not just What/How/When
body:
![](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/e9a157f0-d897-4cdd-bbff-7269d2ebf645/DB23C1A3-38C7-4967-9647-DA65D5E90FB6.png?t=1789762000)

This morning, I was preparing for a podcast with Aimee about AlreadyLoved when a thought landed on me:

**Parents are worship leaders.**

Not because we’re supposed to get our kids singing louder in the backseat.

But because one of the most important things we do as parents is the same thing I’ve spent years trying to do as a worship leader:

**Facilitate encounter.**

For years, I’ve told worship leaders that our job isn’t to make people worship.

We can choose the songs.  
We can create the environment.  
We can invite people to sing.  
We can point toward Jesus.

But we cannot manufacture revelation.

Worship is ultimately a response to seeing God for yourself.

And I’m beginning to think parenting is much the same.

We can teach our children Bible stories.

We can tell them about the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. The God David sang to. The God Paul preached about.

All of that matters.

But somewhere along the way, I want the God we tell them about to become **their God**.

Not simply a concept they inherited from us.

Someone they know.

Someone they’ve spoken to.

Someone they’ve experienced meeting them in fear, disappointment, joy and ordinary Tuesday afternoons.

Because encounter changes things.

When someone has genuinely encountered God, you can’t easily argue that experience out of them.

They may wrestle with church.

They may question things they were taught.

They may even wander for a while.

But somewhere underneath all those questions is a memory:

**I know what it was like when God became real to me.**

That is what I want for my children.

And it has changed the way I think about my role as a parent.

Maybe my job isn’t merely to give them the right information about God.

Maybe I’m also creating little sanctuaries.

Bedtime.

The drive to school.

A conversation after something went wrong.

A prayer whispered when they’re scared.

A moment when they ask a question I don’t have a neat answer for.

Moments where I can come alongside them and say,

*Let’s see where God is in this.*

I cannot make my child encounter God.

Neither can a worship leader.

But I can keep pointing.

I can keep making room.

I can keep helping them notice.

Until, one day, I’m no longer only telling them about the God I know.

They’re telling me about the God **they know**.

Maybe that is one of the most beautiful things parenting can become.

Your lap is their first classroom.

**Let it also be their first chapel.**

**See you next Friday**

Know someone with a preschooler? Share: [AlreadyLovedkids.com](https://AlreadyLovedkids.com?utm_source=letters.batsirai.com&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=your-lap-is-their-first-chapel)

subject: How to know you are healed
previewText: Watching Simmone sing showed me something
body:
![](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/96e19cf4-86d6-4ae7-b9a8-f34fe2a2c6ec/simmone-theRiver.png?t=1790366932)

On this last Tuesday night, I lifted my phone and tried to keep Simmone in the frame.

Our daughter had just joined The River worship team, one of only two new members this year. Now she was singing with them for the first time, in front of thousands of people.

She had the microphone. I had my camera. I was so proud I could hardly keep still.

**What surprised me was what** ***didn’t*** **happen inside me.**

For a long time, being a worship leader was tied to my worth. I’d see someone I knew take the lead on a bigger stage and feel myself shrink. Then I’d quietly shrink their achievement too: *They only got there because they knew someone.*

I hate admitting that. But it’s true.

Watching Simmone, I felt none of it. No calculation about where I should be by now. No wish that I were holding her microphone. I just wanted to catch a good picture of my daughter.

Sometimes you don’t know a wound has healed until something touches it and you don’t flinch.

Later that week, Aimee and I were guests on a couple of podcasts. We talked about getting pregnant in Bible college before we were married. For 26 years, I couldn’t imagine telling that story openly. The shame sat so close to the surface that even thinking about it made my stomach tighten.

But I told it. Aimee was beside me, and the knot wasn’t there.

I don’t think time did that on its own. I’m learning to stand in what Jesus has given me: His righteousness, and a love I don’t have to earn. I can say, “Here is what happened. And here is who God is.” Someone else’s response no longer determines who I am.

That freedom is helping me see my calling more clearly too.

I’ve often thought of myself as *the worship guy*. I love helping people encounter God. I thought the microphone was central to that. But music was one instrument. Songwriting was another. Now I’m finding that creating a children’s book, building with technology, and helping parents make space for their children to meet God are instruments too.

Last week, I wrote about parenting being like leading worship. We can introduce our children to God and make room for them to know Him for themselves. A parent’s lap can become a child’s first chapel.

On Tuesday night, Simmone sang with her own voice. I couldn’t sing her part for her, and I didn’t want to.

I kept my phone up and cheered.

*P.S. That hope is why Aimee and I made* [*AlreadyLoved*](https://alreadylovedkids.com?utm_source=letters.batsirai.com&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=how-to-know-you-are-healed)*. If you know any parents of preschoolers, I’d be grateful if you sent it their way.*  
  
*Oh, and the first episode of one of those podcasts is out:* [https://pod.link/1709107189/episode/ZGViNnkucG9kYmVhbi5jb20vMWFiNmQ1OTUtNDc4MC0zOWJiLTk2YTgtMmNkZjUxZmI4Y2Nk?view=apps&sort=popularity](https://pod.link/1709107189/episode/ZGViNnkucG9kYmVhbi5jb20vMWFiNmQ1OTUtNDc4MC0zOWJiLTk2YTgtMmNkZjUxZmI4Y2Nk?view=apps&sort=popularity&utm_source=letters.batsirai.com&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=how-to-know-you-are-healed)  
  
(Check out the Reel of Simmone here: [https://www.instagram.com/reels/Ddq5ImTubEO/](https://www.instagram.com/reels/Ddq5ImTubEO/?utm_source=letters.batsirai.com&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=how-to-know-you-are-healed))
