subject: I knew them before I met them
body:
![](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/a3e714b4-7fee-489f-ab1d-0140d9c30449/Vintage_Family_Portrait_Framed_in_Warm_Blur.png?t=1790971142)

Me in green, beside my grandmother in pink, with my dad, aunt, and sister. I was eight when we met—but my parents had been introducing us for years. 1983-4

I was eight years old the first time I met my grandmothers.

My grandfathers had already died. My grandmothers were still alive, but they were in Zimbabwe, and it was the early ’80s.

I’d never even spoken to them on the phone.

And yet somehow, I knew them.

When we finally met, they weren’t strangers. It felt like a long-overdue hug.

I’ve been thinking about that.

How could someone I’d never met feel so familiar?

My parents talked about them. They told stories. These women mattered to the people who mattered most to me.

I couldn’t have told you their birthdays or where they went to school. But I knew they had a hand in my parents’ lives. I knew they belonged to us, and we belonged to them.

By the time I met them, there was already a relationship waiting for me.

It makes me wonder what our children hear when we talk about God.

Do they hear about Someone we know?

Someone who matters to us? Someone we speak to, lean on, return to?

Or do they mostly hear things they’re supposed to remember?

There’s a temptation to measure faith by how much we can repeat. The Bible stories. The verses. The right answers.

Those things matter. But knowing the right things about someone isn’t the same as knowing them.

Knowing my grandmother’s second-grade teacher’s name wouldn’t have made that hug feel any more like home.

My parents’ relationship with her did.

And perhaps underneath all the things we’re trying to teach our children, there’s a question they need us to answer:

*Who is Jesus to you?*

Not just what happened long ago.

Who is He in your life now?

The woman at the well had something to tell her town because she’d met Someone. Her words brought people to Jesus. But after spending time with Him, they told her they now believed because they had heard Him for themselves. *(John 4:39–42)* [biblehub.com](https://biblehub.com/niv/john/4-42.htm?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

Her testimony was a bridge.

And people crossed it.

I think about Samuel, too. A boy hearing his name in the night, getting up and running to Eli because he thought Eli was calling.

Eventually, Eli recognized what was happening. He sent Samuel back to lie down and helped him respond if God called again: “Speak, Lord, for your servant is listening.” *(1 Samuel 3:9)* [Bible Gateway](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=I+Samuel+3&version=NIV&utm_source=chatgpt.com)

Eli helped him recognize a voice he didn’t yet know.

There’s something tender about that picture of parenting.

We have stories to tell. We have things to teach. And we get to help our children notice that God is speaking to them, is present with them, and is interested in them.

When the disciples asked Jesus to teach them to pray, His answer began with “Father.” *(Luke 11:1–2)* [Bible Gateway](https://search.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Luke+11&version=NIV%3BNASB&utm_source=chatgpt.com)

Before they said anything else, He gave them Someone to address.

I keep coming back to that.

Who, before what.

Even an AI can repeat what it’s been trained on. It can sound remarkably convincing.

But a convincing answer can’t tell us whether there’s a relationship.  
  
AI, Wikipedia, and the Pharisees can all know the answers to what, how, when, where, even why… but only a relationship can truly answer the question “Who?”

Sure, AI can answer the questions with a name, but that is still just a “what.” What is just the name of the WHO… knowing His name, His words, His facts, and knowing Him in such a way that He would say… and I know you. That’s the only thing that matters.

It makes me listen to my own words.

When I talk about Jesus, am I sharing Someone I know? Or am I repeating things I’ve learned to say?

I want my children to know the Scriptures. I want them to ask questions and understand what they believe.

I also want them to hear me speak about God with the familiarity I heard when my parents spoke about their mothers.

I was eight when I finally met my grandmothers.

But my parents had been introducing us for years.

Remember: Start with WHO.  
  
What's true for kids is true for you too.  
  
See you next Friday…

subject: Lord, If You Had Been Here...
body:
![](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/0b81a34c-f69c-4832-b2cc-e647314319d3/275EA9B2-30CA-4E99-BD35-F7D67B03C793.png?t=1791579493)

*On grief, unanswered questions, and trusting God when nothing makes sense.*

Saturday morning, our son Jaden sent us a message.

His friend’s mother was missing.

Her name was Jolene. We knew her from church. Her daughter had grown up around our kids. We’d served together in drama productions over the years.

I went straight to Twitter and started searching.

An air ambulance traveling from Bermuda to Boston had crashed into the ocean. Jolene was one of the nurses onboard.

At that point, the search was still active. Details were few.

And you know what your mind does in moments like that.

Maybe they’re still out there.

Maybe they’re floating somewhere, holding onto something. Maybe they’ve found a piece of the aircraft to cling to. Maybe someone will spot them.

You know the odds. But you keep hoping.

By the next morning, they’d found the wreckage.

A few hours later, the search was called off.

And just like that, hope had nowhere left to go.

I couldn’t stop thinking about her family.

And the questions.

What happened? Did they know what was happening? Was it quick? Were they afraid?

And then the question underneath all the others.

*Why, God?*

**The woman I knew**

Our church used to put on these fairly large drama productions. They were popular in our city, and I was involved in quite a few of them.

Jolene was often one of the main characters.

She was also an assistant director. She helped get people into their places, kept things moving, gave direction when it was needed, and took some of the weight off the director’s shoulders.

She’d bring donuts for everyone.

It’s funny the things you remember about people.

Not necessarily the big performances or the lines they delivered onstage.

Sometimes it’s the donuts.

The person who noticed that everyone was tired. The person who quietly helped things run smoothly. The steady hand that made everyone else’s job a little easier.

That was Jolene.

She worked as a respiratory therapist, later in our local health network, and eventually became an air ambulance nurse.

Her work took her around the world, helping transport people who needed medical care.

I was reading a Facebook tribute from someone who had worked with her. What struck me was how deeply Jolene had affected this person, and how clearly her faith had been part of that.

Think about the kind of work she did.

Day after day, encountering sickness, emergencies, suffering, and sometimes death.

The very places where people might reasonably ask, *Where is God in all of this?*

And somehow, from what her colleague described, Jolene carried hope into those places.

That stayed with me.

Because this week, I’m asking some of those same questions.

**If You had been here**

I’ve been thinking about Mary and Martha.

Their brother Lazarus had died.

They had sent word to Jesus while Lazarus was still sick. Jesus loved this family. They knew Him. They trusted Him.

And yet He didn’t arrive in time.

When Martha finally saw Him, she said:

“Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died.”

Mary would later say the same thing.

I wonder how many of us have prayed some version of that sentence.

Lord, if You had been there, that plane wouldn’t have gone down.

If You had been there, those children would still have their mother.

If You had been there, we wouldn’t be having this conversation.

I don’t think those are necessarily questions of unbelief.

Sometimes they’re the questions of people who know God is good, know He is able, and cannot understand why He didn’t do what they know He could have done.

I think that’s what makes grief so difficult for people of faith.

We aren’t just wrestling with what happened.

We’re wrestling with what happened in a world where God is present, loving, and powerful.

And sometimes those truths feel terribly difficult to hold together.

**This is not how it should be**

Years ago, Steven Curtis Chapman lost his young daughter in a tragic accident.

He later made an album called *Beauty Will Rise*, born out of that grief.

I’ve been thinking about the tension in those songs.

The ache of saying, “Lord, this isn’t how it was supposed to be.”

And yet somehow, still turning toward Him.

I think there’s a kind of faith that can only exist in that tension.

Not the faith that says everything worked out.

Not the faith that has found an explanation that makes the pain acceptable.

But the faith that says:

This is not what I wanted.

This is not what I would have chosen.

If I were God, I would have chosen something different.

Yet here we are.

And I still trust You.

I still love You.

I still believe You are good.

I’m not sure I can explain that kind of faith. And I certainly don’t want to make it sound easier than it is.

Especially not to a family that is waking up each morning to a world without someone they love.

But I keep coming back to something in the story of Lazarus.

**Jesus wept**

Jesus knew what He was going to do.

He knew Lazarus would rise.

And yet, when He came to the tomb and saw Mary weeping, and the people around her weeping, He was deeply moved.

And then we get those two remarkable words.

**Jesus wept.**

He didn’t stand outside the tomb and tell everyone to cheer up because everything was going to be fine.

He didn’t explain the larger purposes of God.

He wept.

The One who knew resurrection was coming still entered into the grief of the people He loved.

I find that incredibly comforting.

Because sometimes I think we imagine faith means getting to a place where the pain doesn’t hurt so much. Where we can explain what God is doing. Where we can confidently tell people that everything happens for a reason.

But Jesus didn’t seem interested in explaining away their tears.

He joined them.

And maybe that’s where we begin.

Not with answers.

But with the God who weeps with us.

**Lord, help my unbelief**

I’ve also been thinking about how easily I can turn God into a kind of superhero.

Someone who is supposed to swoop in whenever life becomes dangerous or painful and make everything right.

And He does rescue us. He does save. Again and again.

But He has never promised that loving Him means we will be spared every tragedy.

I know that in my head.

It’s much harder to know it in my heart when someone I know has died.

I believe there is so much more to God’s understanding, His purposes, and His perspective than I can begin to comprehend.

I believe one day we will see Him face to face.

But I don’t know why this happened.

I don’t know why Jolene was on that flight.

I don’t know why her family has to endure this.

And I don’t want to pretend I do.

I think of what Jesus said to Thomas:

“Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.”

Maybe that’s where I find myself today.

Not seeing.

Not understanding.

But wanting to believe.

Believing that He is good, even when I cannot make sense of what has happened.

Believing that His love is not measured by whether He prevents every painful thing from touching my life.

Believing that nothing, not even death, can separate us from His love.

And when my belief feels small, I can borrow the prayer of another desperate father in the Gospels:

**“I believe; help my unbelief!”**

**Thank You for Jolene**

I’ve been thinking about those donuts again.

And the drama rehearsals.

And all the people Jolene helped over the years, many of whom we’ll probably never know.

The patients she cared for. The families she helped. The colleagues who saw something of her faith in the middle of difficult days.

What a beautiful thing to leave behind.

Not just memories of what you accomplished, but memories of how you loved people.

I am grateful that I got to know her, even in the small way I did.

And my heart breaks for her family.

Lord, thank You for Jolene.

Thank You for her life, her faith, her service, and the light she carried into places where hope must sometimes have been difficult to find.

Be near to her family in ways that words cannot accomplish.

And forgive us when we feel we must explain what we cannot understand.

Teach us to grieve with those who grieve.

To love while we have the opportunity.

To hold one another a little closer.

And to trust You, even here.

Especially here.

I don’t have an answer for why that plane went down.

I wish I did.

But I keep coming back to Jesus standing outside the tomb of someone He loved.

Knowing what was coming.

And weeping anyway.

Perhaps today, that’s enough for me to hold onto.

See you next Friday.

subject: They Don't Swim Great to Become a Dolphin
previewText: They swim great because they are dolphins.
body:
![](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/6c15d8b2-82b2-48ae-9c1c-14f1675e0783/Dolphin_gliding_through_sunlit_blue.png?t=1792178346)

I was working on a newsletter about identity when my Apple TV screensaver came on.

Dolphins swimming through the ocean.

I stopped to watch. There was something beautiful about the way they moved. So graceful. So effortless.

They weren’t trying to impress anybody.

But it was impressive.

They were just expressing their nature.

And this thought came to me:

**You’re not swimming to become a dolphin. You’re swimming because you are one.**

I wonder how often I get that backward. Doing things to become somebody. Looking to what I accomplish, and how people respond, to tell me who I am.

Even something I love can become a way of asking, *Am I enough?*

Singing. Creating. Building something.

There’s a difference between enjoying someone’s response to what I’ve made and needing their response before I can enjoy it myself.

I think that’s the difference I’m reaching for between performance and expression.

Performance keeps looking outward. Did they like it? Were they impressed? Was it enough?

Expression finds satisfaction in bringing something from within into the world. There’s joy in the singing itself. In finding the words. In making something that feels true to how you were made.

Applause is lovely. But it doesn’t have to decide whether the thing was worth doing.

There’s a line in *Chariots of Fire* a quote of Eric Liddel that I’ve always loved:

“God made me fast. And when I run, I feel His pleasure.”

I love that the pleasure is in the running.

Notice that it wasn’t in the winning.   
  
Imagine him saying, “When I win, I feel his pleasure.”   
Sounds like many a hockey or pageant mom today…   
  
Now he does go on to say “to win is to honor Him”, but I don't think he means that to come second or lose is to dishonor God.   
  
The point is, God’s pleasure is in the expression, not the performance. Like any 'normal’ parent!

Reminds me of a lyric in the AlreadyLoved song:  
  
“He doesn’t want you to perform, He just loves to hear you sing”

As parents watching a child play soccer or sing at a school concert, we want them to do well. You can cheer when they score.

But sometimes the thing that makes you smile is simply watching them out there. Recognizing their little mannerisms. Seeing their face light up.

That’s your child.

Their delight becomes your delight.

I wonder if I leave enough room for God to enjoy me that way. Whether I’m so busy asking Him to assess what I’ve done that I miss the possibility that He’s delighting in me as I do it.

Back on the screen, the dolphins kept swimming.

Imagine one of them trying to walk around on the shore. Watching other creatures. Practicing. Trying to get better.

Maybe it becomes the best walking dolphin anyone has ever seen.

Then you see that same dolphin in the water.

There it is.

The movement. The freedom. The beauty that all that walking practice could never quite produce.

It makes me wonder how much energy we spend becoming good at things we think will make us valuable. How often we mistake approval for the feeling of being fully alive.

“Stop doing. Start being.”

Those words have been coming to me lately. I’m beginning to understand what I mean by them.

I still want to work, create, sing, build, and get better at things. There’s joy in learning to express something well.

But I don’t want everything I do to carry the responsibility of proving that I’m somebody.

Before I sing a note, I’m already loved. After the song ends, I’m still loved.

Maybe knowing that lets me enjoy the singing more and offer it more freely. Lets someone else be better at it without making me feel smaller.

The dolphins weren’t waiting for a verdict.

I was watching them, delighted.

And they just kept swimming.

[You are AlreadyLoved](https://alreadylovedkids.com?utm_source=letters.batsirai.com&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=they-don-t-swim-great-to-become-a-dolphin).

See you next Friday

subject: God Almighty, Let Men Spit in His Face
body:
![](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/20336980-2e03-48d0-8ba7-c7e7901d9bb8/Cinematic_Sunset_Crucifixion_Scene.png?t=1792787665)

Imagine the son of a king walking up to his father in public.

In front of everyone, he slaps him across the face.

Then he spits in his face.

Before the king can even react, the royal guards rush forward. Within seconds, they're ready to seize the young man.

But the king raises his hand.

"Leave him."

The guards stop.

Not because the son has done nothing wrong. Not because the insult doesn't matter. And certainly not because the king lacks the power to punish him.

**But because he's his son.**

The relationship changes everything.

Now imagine that same king watching someone brutally beat his beloved son.

He has the power to stop it. An entire army stands ready to act at his command.

But again, he raises his hand.

And again, the guards stand down.

Only this time, the people he's showing mercy to are the very ones hurting his son.

What kind of love would make a father do that?

I read a sentence recently that stopped me.

**God Almighty let men spit in His face.**

I've been sitting with that thought.

The God who spoke the universe into existence allowed men to mock Him, whip Him, slap Him, and spit in His face.

And the part that really gets me isn't just that Jesus endured it.

It's that the Father allowed it.

Think about that for a moment.

Imagine watching someone beat your son. Not just insult him, but whip him, drive thorns into his head, and eventually nail him to a cross.

What would it take for you not to intervene?

Now imagine having all the power in the universe to stop it.

Jesus said He could ask His Father for more than twelve legions of angels.

In other words, there was no shortage of power to put an end to what was happening.

And yet, the Father restrained Himself.

Why?

I keep coming back to this thought.

**Mercy is love in restraint.**

We often think of mercy as God withholding what we deserve.

But what if mercy is also God revealing who He is?

What if, in the Father's restraint, we're seeing something about His heart toward the very people doing this to His Son?

### What if He sees us as family?

I've heard people say that God isn't our Father until we accept Jesus into our hearts.

And I understand that Scripture speaks of becoming children of God through faith. I'm not dismissing that.

But I can't get past the fatherly disposition God demonstrates toward people who haven't yet believed, who haven't repented, who don't even recognize Him.

Especially at the cross.

Here are men doing unspeakable things to His beloved Son.

They are not worshipping Him. They're mocking Him.

They're not asking for forgiveness. They're gambling for His clothes.

They don't even know who He is.

And the Son prays:

*"Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing."* — Luke 23:34

I find that prayer astonishing.

Jesus isn't pretending the violence doesn't matter. He isn't calling their actions harmless.

He's asking for forgiveness for people who don't even understand the magnitude of what they've done.

It's as though He's saying, *Father, they don't know. They don't know who they're hurting. They don't know what they're doing.*

And I can't help wondering whether that prayer reveals something we've missed about God's heart.

After all, Jesus told us to love our enemies. To bless those who curse us. To turn the other cheek.

He told us that our Father in heaven sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous.

He was revealing what the Father is like.

And now, at Calvary, He's living it.

**The very people who are hurting Him are the people He came to save.**

The Father isn't looking at humanity as something disposable. Something He made that has gone terribly wrong and can simply be destroyed.

These are people He loves.

People made in His image.

People who have rejected Him, misunderstood Him, and wounded the One He sent to rescue them.

And still, He loves them.

It's one thing to show mercy to someone who loves you.

It's another thing entirely to show mercy to someone who is driving nails through your Son's hands.

### This was always His heart

What strikes me even more is that none of this caught God by surprise.

Peter tells us that Christ was chosen before the foundation of the world.

Before the world existed, before humanity sinned, before the first whip was raised or the first nail driven, God already knew the cost of loving us.

And He came anyway.

This wasn't a reluctant Father being persuaded by a merciful Son.

The Father Himself so loved the world that He gave His only Son.

The cross wasn't Jesus changing the Father's mind about humanity.

**It was Jesus revealing the Father's heart toward humanity.**

And suddenly Paul's words carry a different weight:

*"But God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us."* — Romans 5:8

While we were still sinners.

Not after we repented.

Not after we understood.

Not after we loved Him back.

**While we were still sinners.**

We didn't become loved when we recognized Him.

We were loved even when we rejected Him.

And that makes me wonder whether we've sometimes made God's fatherly love sound like a reward for accepting Him, rather than the very reason He came looking for us.

I think there's a difference between entering into the life of sonship through Christ and discovering the Father whose love was already reaching toward us.

The invitation to become children of God doesn't mean He was indifferent to us before we believed.

Calvary tells me something very different.

It tells me that while we were still His enemies, His heart was already turned toward us in love.

### Mercy is love in restraint

There's something extraordinary about a father who has the power to intervene but chooses mercy.

Not because the wrongdoing is insignificant.

Not because the suffering doesn't matter.

But because the people involved matter to him.

And I think that's what I see when I look at Calvary.

I see a Father who loves His Son beyond anything I can imagine.

And I see that same Father loving the people who are killing Him.

The Father doesn't cease loving His Son in order to love humanity. Father and Son are united in the love that makes this sacrifice possible.

That is the mystery of the cross.

God doesn't excuse the violence. He bears its cost.

He doesn't pretend evil isn't evil. He overcomes it with love.

And Jesus, the perfect revelation of the Father, turns the other cheek.

Not because He has no power to respond.

But because love has chosen another way.

**The restraint of God is not the absence of power. It is the presence of love.**

I wonder how much of our picture of God would change if we began there.

Not with a God demanding to be recognized.

Not with a God waiting for humanity to become worthy of His affection.

But with a Father whose heart has always been turned toward us.

A Father who can look upon the very people harming His beloved Son and still desire their forgiveness.

A Father whose love was not awakened by our repentance, but whose love made our repentance possible.

I don't think I'll ever read that scene quite the same way again.

Because perhaps the most astonishing thing about Calvary is not only what humanity was willing to do to God.

It's what God was willing to endure for humanity.

God Almighty let men spit in His face.

And the mercy that held back His hand was revealing His heart all along.

*I am your Father.*

*And though you slay Me, I will still love you.*

subject: It's Easy With You
body:
![](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/de241ab5-6e6c-4b5b-96b7-8d05e98a4ab9/Moses_supported_by_Aaron_and_Hur.png?t=1793394335)

This is how I fight my battles…

After high school, about fifteen of us in Zimbabwe were dreaming of going abroad for university.

It was a big dream. And an expensive one.

There were applications to complete, schools to get into, and funding to find. We didn’t have all the answers, and the whole thing felt overwhelming.

So we would meet in a park downtown and pray together.

There wasn’t a grand agenda. We’d share updates about the schools we were applying to, encourage one another, and pray about the challenges we were facing.

Looking back, I think twelve out of the fifteen of us got into the schools we wanted, received funding, and found a way forward.

When I tell that story now, it almost sounds easy.

It didn’t feel easy when we were living it.

I’ve been thinking about that lately because I’m wondering how much harder I make life when I try to live it without depending on the Lord.

I know how to bring Him the big things. Healing. An impossible situation. A prayer that requires enormous faith.

But somewhere between those moments, I slip back into figuring things out on my own.

My wife, Aimee, and I were praying about that this morning.

We’ve been building [AlreadyLoved](https://alreadylovedkids.com?utm_source=letters.batsirai.com&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=it-s-easy-with-you) to help parents introduce their children to God and help them see themselves the way He sees them.

Some people dismiss it as AI slop. Others love it because they can see what it might mean for a child to hear, again and again, what God believes about them.

And I find myself wondering: What kind of world would this be if children everywhere grew up knowing that?

It’s a beautiful dream.

But then I start thinking about everything it will take to get there.

I have to learn marketing. Solve the next problem. Find money we don’t have. Figure out how to make it all work.

And somewhere in there, everything gets tight and desperate.

I start carrying a dream about helping children know God as though it’s entirely up to me to make it happen.

This morning, as Aimee and I prayed, I found myself coming back to a simple thought:

*Lord, I want to do this with You.*

Not just for You. Not just in Your name.

With You.

I want to hear Your voice and Your thoughts. I want Your motives to become mine. I want to know what it looks like to work alongside You, even when the work in front of me is learning marketing or looking at our finances.

I think about Moses standing above the battle with his hands raised. When his hands were lifted, Israel prevailed. When they came down, the battle turned. And when he grew tired, Aaron and Hur came alongside him and held up his arms.

I can’t help seeing in that picture a posture of dependence.

I’m used to thinking of worship and work as two separate things. I can pray, lift my hands, and then get back to “real life”—back to the decisions and responsibilities.

But what if I could bring that same posture into the work?

Jesus says His yoke is easy and His burden is light.

And I keep wondering: Does that apply to the ordinary parts of my life too?

Is business easier in His presence? Parenting? Finances? What about healing, freedom, and the places where we need deliverance?

I struggle to think of one thing that isn’t better when it’s done with Him.

That doesn’t mean everything happens quickly or turns out the way I want. The applications in Zimbabwe still had to be filled out. The funding still had to be found. We still had to wait for answers.

But in that park, we brought our hopes and uncertainties to God, and we held them together.

And I wonder how much of what feels heavy in my life right now feels that way because I’m trying to do it *for* Him without actually doing it *with* Him.

Not just believing He’s there. But leaning on Him. Talking with Him. Listening. Trusting Him with the outcome.

Leaning on my Beloved.

I also wonder if we sometimes think the only spiritual question is, “Lord, what do You want me to do?”

That’s a question worth asking. But I wonder if He also wants to hear what’s on our hearts. What we want to build. What we’re dreaming about. What we’re afraid might not work.

And perhaps His invitation is, *Can we do this together?*

That’s what I’m learning to ask about Already Loved. I still catch myself slipping back into striving, picking up the weight as if I’m the only one carrying it.

But I can return to that prayer:

***God, I want to do this with You.***

What are you trying to figure out or carry right now?

What might it look like to do it with Him?  
  
**See you next Friday.**

subject: It's Not What You Know. It's Who You Know.
body:
# 

![](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/ebf47238-e129-4cdf-a27e-57f3918d5972/3amPickup.png?t=1793998679)

I've been thinking about that old saying:

"It's not what you know. It's who you know."

We usually say it when someone gets a job because they know the right person, or gets an opportunity because of a personal connection.

And we all understand how that works.

I can know everything about Elon Musk. I can read his biography, watch his interviews, study his companies, and follow him on X.

But none of that means I know him.

I know *about* him.

Now, if I actually knew him personally, that would be a completely different story.

The same goes for the CEO of a company I want to work for. I could know everything on their LinkedIn profile, but a personal relationship with them would open doors that all that information couldn't.

Because the favour isn't in the information.

**The favour is in the relationship with the person. Grace.**

And I've been realizing how much this applies to almost everything in life.

Especially now, in the age of AI.

For generations, we've built an economy around what people know.

You go to school, study, get a degree, maybe a PhD, and your knowledge sets you apart. People pay you because you know something they don't.

But now?

I have something that feels like a PhD in almost every discipline sitting in my pocket.

I can ask AI how to write code, start a business, understand a contract, learn a language, or solve a problem that would have required an expensive consultant just a few years ago.

And it's only getting better.

Suddenly, knowing a lot isn't quite the advantage it used to be.

Knowledge still matters, of course. But access to knowledge is becoming less and less scarce.

So what becomes valuable when everyone has access to the same information?

I think it's the person.

Their perspective. Their judgment. Their creativity. Their relationships. The unique way they see the world.

**Not just what they know, but who they are.**

And the funny thing is, I think it's always been this way.

We're just beginning to see it.

Which brings me to Jesus.

### Do you know Him, or do you know His LinkedIn profile?

Imagine I asked two people to tell me about Jesus.

The first person gets up and says:

"Well, He was born of a virgin about 2,000 years ago. He performed miracles, taught the disciples, died on a cross for our sins, and rose again on the third day."

Wonderful.

All true. All important.

But that's His LinkedIn profile.

I want to know who He is.

Imagine another person gets up and says:

"Well, I was talking to Him this morning. I've been so busy lately, and I felt Him inviting me to slow down and just spend some time with Him.

"I was worried about a project I'm working on, and as I talked to Him about it, I began to see it differently.

"And then there were some responsibilities I hadn't followed up on, and I was getting stressed. I felt Him reminding me that yes, I needed to take care of them, but I didn't have to carry the anxiety alone.

"And there are some things I'm honestly afraid of. Things I don't know how to do. Things I don't even want to do.

"But I can tell Him that. I don't have to pretend.

"He's my friend."

Do you see the difference?

One person can tell me what Jesus did.

The other is telling me who Jesus is *to them*.

And I wonder how often we've confused the two.

We've become very good at teaching ourselves and our children Jesus' LinkedIn profile.

We teach the stories, the miracles, the commandments, the facts.

And those things matter. They really do.

But when was the last time you spoke to Him?

Not just read about Him.

Spoke to Him.

When was the last time you brought Him into a problem you were trying to solve, or a decision you were afraid to make?

When was the last time you just enjoyed being with Him?

Because I don't think Jesus came merely to give us more information about God.

**He came to introduce us to His Father.**

### Even the devil knew Scripture.

There's a moment in the wilderness where the devil tempts Jesus by quoting Scripture.

He takes words from Psalm 91 and tells Jesus to throw Himself down from the temple because God has promised that His angels will protect Him.

Think about that.

The devil knew the Scripture.

Jesus knew the Scripture.

Same words.

But they saw them completely differently.

Jesus wasn't simply responding with a better Bible verse. He knew the Father whose heart those words revealed.

And I find it fascinating that just before the wilderness, at His baptism, Jesus had heard His Father declare:

"This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased."

Then the temptation comes:

"If You are the Son of God..."

Jesus knew who He was.

He knew whose He was.

And that changed how He understood everything.

The words mattered. But the relationship gave them meaning.

**Knowledge in the hands of someone who knows the Father is different from knowledge in the hands of someone who doesn't.**

And suddenly, I see that old saying everywhere.

In worship, it's not just about knowing the right songs or the right chords. It's knowing the One we're singing to.

In parenting, it's not just about teaching our children Bible stories. It's helping them know the God those stories reveal.

In business, it's not just about knowing all the strategies and techniques. It's about the perspective we bring, the people we serve, the relationships we build, and learning to work *with* God rather than simply *for* Him.

Even with the projects I'm working on, I'm beginning to see that I don't have to know how to do everything before I begin.

I can lean on Someone who knows me, loves me, and is willing to walk through it with me.

It's not what you know.

It's who you know.

And here's the part I really love:

**That includes yourself.**

Because as AI makes knowledge more accessible, I think we're going to be confronted with a question many of us have spent our whole lives avoiding.

Who am I, apart from what I know?

Apart from what I can do?

Apart from what I can produce, achieve, or prove?

What do I bring into the world that isn't simply a collection of information?

I think the answer begins with identity.

Knowing who you are. Knowing whose you are. And living from that place.

Maybe that's part of the gift hidden in this whole AI revolution. It's forcing us to reconsider what makes a person valuable.

And perhaps we'll discover that our value was never primarily in how much we knew.

It was always in who we were.

### The Jesus who answers at 3 a.m.

I want to come back to something, though.

Because I don't want us to turn knowing Jesus into another strategy for getting ahead.

As if He's just the most influential connection we could possibly have.

I mean something much more personal than that.

Do you know the Jesus you can call at three in the morning?

The Jesus who would come and get you when you've made another terrible decision and need someone to take you home?

The Jesus you can tell, "I'm afraid. I don't know what I'm doing. I don't even want to do this."

The Jesus who isn't shocked by your mess, intimidated by your questions, or waiting for you to impress Him before He welcomes you.

Not just the Jesus who died for you 2,000 years ago.

The Jesus who loves you right now.

Who wants to walk with you today.

Who wants to be known, not merely studied.

That Jesus.

**That Jesus.**

Do you know Him?

subject: Defining Encounter
body:
# 

![](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/015a6d66-bf68-4faa-823f-a4763530cd3f/Sunset_Companions_on_the_Porch.png?t=1794596186)

A photo from last year popped up on my phone recently.

Last November, I was in Dallas speaking at a worship conference. While I was there, I said something that I later shared on social media:

**“Every time we gather, we should expect an encounter.”**

![](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/86638dd2-7f01-4bd9-a9d4-7d2cb0d75c21/Every_time_we_gather__we_should_expect_an_encounter.png?t=1794596132)

A year later, there it was again - you know how Google Photos will show you images from a year ago? I digress.

And as I read them, I realized something.

I still believe what I said. But I don't think I mean quite the same thing anymore.

At the time, I was thinking about those remarkable moments we have with the Lord. Moments when His presence seems so tangible. Moments that mark us, change us, sometimes for the rest of our lives.

I wanted everyone to know that those encounters were possible every time we gathered.

And when they didn't happen, well, we would keep contending for more.

I still want those moments. I still believe we can expect God to do extraordinary things.

But something has been changing in the way I see encounter.

**I think I was defining encounter by what happened, rather than Who I was meeting.**

Think about it.

If a friend invites me to his house, I expect to encounter him when I get there.

I expect to see him, talk with him, look him in the eyes, and simply be with him.

Some visits might be profound. We might have a conversation that changes my life.

Other times, we might just sit on the couch and watch TV.

But I wouldn't leave his house saying I hadn't encountered him because nothing extraordinary happened.

I was with him.

And then I started thinking about what it would feel like to be on the other side.

Imagine someone comes to visit me, and every time they leave, all they talk about is what they received.

"He paid for dinner."

"He gave me a check."

"He bought me a car."

"He made me feel amazing."

Now, those are all wonderful things. And I might have been delighted to give them.

But if that's all they ever talked about, I think eventually I'd begin to wonder whether they actually wanted to be with me, or just wanted what I could give them.

Now imagine my child comes over for lunch.

Someone asks, "How was lunch with your dad?"

"It was great!"

"Oh yeah? What did you do?"

"Nothing much. We just hung out. Had lunch. Talked. It was really good."

No extraordinary event. No gift to show for it.

**"I just wanted to be with Dad."**

There's something so beautiful about that.

The relationship itself was enough.

And I wonder if sometimes, even in our genuine hunger for more of God, we can become so focused on what happens in His presence that we overlook the joy of simply being with Him.

We talk about what we felt. What we received. How we were healed, changed, encouraged, or blessed.

And those are wonderful things. They're worth celebrating.

But what if the greatest thing about being in His presence isn't what happens to us?

**What if it's simply that we're with Him?**

I'm beginning to see how much changes when we look at things through a relational lens rather than a legalistic one.

The same words begin to mean something different.

If encounter is an experience, then no, I can't guarantee it. I can't manufacture it. I can't make something extraordinary happen every time we gather.

But if encounter is meeting with a Person, that's different.

And I think this is what worship is really about.

An intentional turning aside.

A moment when we stop what we're doing and give Him our attention.

Not because that's when God arrives. Not because the music somehow brings Him into the room.

But because He is already here.

Emmanuel. God with us.

And perhaps there's a beautiful freedom in that.

We can still hunger for healing, miracles, revelation, and all those extraordinary moments with Him.

But we don't have to make those experiences the measure of whether we've encountered Him.

We can simply enjoy being with Him.

The experience may be extraordinary or ordinary.

**The Person never is.**

And so, a year later, I look at that photograph and find myself saying exactly the same thing.

Only now, it means something different.

*Every time we gather, we should expect an encounter.*

Not because something extraordinary is guaranteed to happen.

But because Someone extraordinary is already with us.

See you next Friday.  
  
*Would love it if you could tell someone about this, or forward this newsletter on… and thanks to those of you who already do (*😉*)*

subject: Thank God for Normal
body:
![](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/4f9047a1-ce89-4284-a506-942cdd034db9/An_Ordinary_Day__A_Gift.png?t=1795213516)

“Back to life as normal.”

After a great weekend away, we say it with a sigh. Back to work. Back to laundry. Back to figuring out what’s for dinner.

But get sick, hurt yourself, or spend a few nights wondering how you’ll pay the rent, and those same words sound like a prayer.

*God, I just want things to be normal again.*

I keep thinking about that. How something we’re so eager to escape can become the very thing we long for.

It’s easy to recognize God on the mountaintop. At a conference, a concert, a night of worship when everything feels alive. And in the valley, when we’re frightened or desperate, we reach for Him.

But so much of life is lived in the middle.

School. Work. Dishes. Pickleball. Worship practice. Walking the dog. Watching something on Netflix before bed.

We can’t live on the mountaintop. We don’t want to live in the valley. But I’m beginning to appreciate the plains.

There’s room to do life here. Raise a family. Make dinner. Have a friend over. Nothing remarkable to report when someone asks how the week has been.

Oh, to be so fortunate.

I don’t want to need a crisis to recognize the blessing of an ordinary day. And I don’t want to spend so much time looking forward to the next extraordinary encounter with God that I overlook His presence in the life I already have.

He’s here, too.

In the kitchen. On the drive to work. On the same route the dog insists on sniffing as though he’s never been there before.

And I can talk with Him here. About what’s on my mind. What’s frustrating me. Something funny. Something I’m grateful for. There doesn’t have to be an emergency.

I think about friendship. How much of it grows through ordinary time together. Going for a walk. Sharing a meal. Talking while you do something else.

Because of Jesus, we are already loved sons and daughters. We belong. And within that belonging is this beautiful invitation to know Him. To grow familiar with His company as we walk through our days.

That’s what I want our kids to discover, too. They can know God while their life is still school and snacks and bedtime. They can talk to Him about the day they actually had.

I still love the mountaintop. And when I’m in the valley, I’ll still pray for a way through.

But today, I’m thinking about the plains.

Dinner to make. A dog to walk.

And God, here with me.  
  
**See you next Friday.**
